From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.

backups.overview: Horseshoe Peak (8,480+ ft per the 1963 USGS Cascade Pass quad) is the high point of Ripsaw Ridge, a knife-edge arête connecting Boston Peak to Mt. Buckner, about a quarter-mile west of Buckner's summit, on the Skagit/Chelan county line deep in the Cascade Pass / Sahale Arm high country of North Cascades NP. With only ~80 ft of prominence it's really a subsidiary tower on the ridge rather than a standalone peak, but it made the Bulgers' Washington Top 100 list on the strength of its height and named status. It's rated an easy Grade II, 5.2 rock climb: mostly loose Class 3 scrambling with one short, exposed 5th-class step through a notch just below the true summit. Most parties combine it with Sahale Peak and/or Mt. Buckner in a single long day or overnight, since all three share the same Sahale Arm / Horseshoe Basin approach.
backups.beta: From Sahale Glacier Camp (or a Horseshoe Basin camp), cross into Horseshoe Basin, gain the base of a class 3 dike/gully system below Ripsaw Ridge, and follow it (with a short class 4 step) up to the ridge crest near the 'Lick of Flame' spire. From there a narrow ramp leads to the summit; it begins as 3rd-class terrain and turns into a short section of 5th-class (5.2) climbing in its final ~100 ft below the top. Rope up for this last section — most parties treat it as one roughly 100-ft pitch. Descend by a single rappel off a horn on the summit (backed by old fixed webbing) or downclimb the same dike/ramp system, then retrace the approach.
backups.turnaround: This is a short technical objective on an exposed, remote summit block with a long approach — sources stress climbing it only in a solid weather window and being willing to back off the ramp before storms or high winds move in, since retreat from the upper ramp requires careful downclimbing or a rappel rather than a quick walk-off.
backups.rappels: 1 single-rope rappel down the south face from the summit (some parties instead downclimb the class 3–4 dike/gully back into Horseshoe Basin)
backups.face: South side / Horseshoe Basin face of Ripsaw Ridge
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No reliable cell service in the Cascade Pass / Sahale / Horseshoe Basin backcountry; a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) is recommended for this remote North Cascades objective.
backups.descent: From the summit notch, downclimb or make a short lower/rappel back through the 5.2 crux to the ledge below (a 30m rope is enough in dry summer conditions; carry more, or plan a full-length rappel, if snow/ice forces a higher start — no fixed anchors are reported, so build off a slung horn or chockstone). Reverse the Class 3/3+ terrain — dihedral slab, notch, rock spur — back to the saddle above Horseshoe Basin, then reverse whichever approach you used: back up and over Sahale Arm to Cascade Pass, or back up through Horseshoe/Pelton Basin to Cascade Pass.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the 23-mile Cascade River Road out of Marblemount; NPS wilderness permit (with bear canister for overnight) required, no day-use fee inside the park.
waypoints.directions: The final miles of Cascade River Road out of Marblemount are unpaved and washboarded, and high clearance or AWD makes the drive to the road end considerably easier.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass and turns east toward Pelton/Horseshoe Basin; a signed spur drops 1 mi and 800 ft to Doubtful Lake below the Sahale Arm.
waypoints.directions: Take the Cascade Pass Trail's well-graded switchbacks up the valley headwall, about 1,800 ft of gain on the only fully maintained tread of the route. Everything above the pass is unmaintained, loose and cairn-marked by comparison, so cover this section efficiently.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: Highest established backcountry camp in the park, at the base of Sahale Glacier; wind-wall rock sites, reservable NPS permit required, snowmelt water only early season.
waypoints.directions: Continue past the pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail and climb the open heather ridge, passing the Doubtful Lake overlook, to the camp at the toe of the glacier. It is a steady 2,200 ft of exposed, shadeless climbing with no water until you reach camp.

waypoints.name: Secret Gully descent off Sahale Arm
waypoints.note: Climbers' descent gully dropping east off the Sahale Arm into Horseshoe Basin; loose rock on slabs and unstable underfoot once snow-free.
waypoints.directions: From camp, traverse east across the boulder-and-heather plateau below the glacier, passing the dozen or so established camp pads, then downclimb a steep snowfield that can stay firm or icy into midsummer — an axe or whippet earns its place here. Traverse east again to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge, then follow the cairned climbers' trail down the ridge over one short 4th-class step to where the gully drops away east.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Basin staging area
waypoints.note: Waterfall-lined cirque beneath Ripsaw Ridge between Boston Peak and Buckner; stage here before the scramble up to Horseshoe Peak's south-facing gully.
waypoints.directions: Descend the scree-and-talus gully to the snowfield at about 6,600 ft and cross it into the basin. Melted out, the gully is loose mostly-3rd-class ground that needs real care; with snow still in it the concern shifts to steep firm snow instead. In the basin, traverse the wide ledge at roughly 6,600 ft as it rises toward the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine near 6,800 ft. Do not drink the basin's water — it drains historic mine tailings, so carry what you need from Doubtful Creek or camp.

waypoints.name: Summit gully and ledge
waypoints.note: 30-45° loose gully climbs to a ledge about 100 ft below the true summit, directly below the final 5.2 notch.
waypoints.directions: Contour northeast and then east on loose scree, talus and slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge under the peak, then start up the Class 3 dike-and-gully system. A short Class 4 step breaks it partway up. The whole line is loose enough that another party above you is the main hazard, so wear a helmet and keep the group either tight or well out of the fall line.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Peak
waypoints.note: True summit gained by ~5 ft of 5th-class climbing to a one-meter-square notch (feels overhung but isn't); downclimb or single-rope rappel to reverse.
waypoints.directions: From the ledge, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 onto a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the top, exiting on loose Class 3/4 rock at the notch. The final moves are 5.2 over fall-would-be-fatal exposure, so most parties rope the ramp as one pitch of roughly 30 m and belay off the horn on the east side of the notch. That horn is also the rappel anchor on the way down; it is natural rock with no fixed hardware, so carry a few cams in case the sling is missing or worn.

backups.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack is sufficient for the single technical pitch — a small-to-mid set of cams and a few stoppers/slings for gear placements and to back up the summit rap anchor; some solo/small parties have rope-soloed or simul-climbed the short pitch with a 60m rope.
pro_tips: Plan the approach carefully — glacier travel may be involved depending on route
Often combined with neighboring summits given the effort to get there
watch_out: Rock is notoriously chossy — test every hold, especially in the gully and on the dihedral slab
The summit notch has only ~5 ft of 5th-class climbing but a fall there would be fatal; place a small cam/stopper at the belay even though it's short
It's easy to lose the correct line through Horseshoe Basin's talus back to the saddle in poor visibility — note landmarks on the way in
Early-season snow bridges/moats near the Sahale Glacier require caution and self-arrest readiness
backups.pro_needs: A few small cams (~0.3-0.75) and a set of stoppers protect the short 5.2 crux near the summit notch; good small cam placements and solid stopper constrictions have both been reported. No fixed anchors — use a slung horn or chockstone for the rappel/lower.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through September for the standard scramble; the access road itself often isn't fully open until late June, so earlier attempts are rare. Some climbers prefer going right after the road opens (Late June-early July) when residual snow makes the Sahale Arm/Horseshoe Basin traverse easier underfoot; by August it's mostly bare talus. A first reported winter ascent (Feb 2024) climbed the SE face as M3 mixed/ice terrain with rime-covered rock — well outside the standard summer objective and requiring a full ice/mixed rack.
backups.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of the Cascade River Road — gravel/washboard, high-clearance/AWD recommended), climb the well-graded Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks 3.7 mi and about 1,800 ft to the broad 5,400-ft saddle at Cascade Pass. Two standard lines converge on Horseshoe Peak from here, both eventually crossing loose, unmaintained terrain above the pass. Sahale Arm option: continue past the Cascade Pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail, climbing the open heather ridge past the Doubtful Lake overlook to Sahale Glacier Camp (about 5.9 mi and 3,940 ft of gain from the trailhead, ~7,600 ft). From camp, traverse east across the boulder/heather plateau below Sahale Glacier (passing roughly a dozen established camp pads), downclimb a steep snowfield (whippet or axe useful, can be firm/icy into midsummer), then traverse east to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge. Follow a cairned climber's trail down the ridge, negotiating one short 4th-class step, into a scree/talus gully that drops to a snowfield around 6,600 ft. Cross this snowfield into Horseshoe Basin, traverse a wide ledge at ~6,600 ft rising gradually to ~6,800 ft at the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine, then continue on loose scree/talus contouring to a stance south/southeast of Horseshoe Peak below the crest of Ripsaw Ridge. Lower Horseshoe Basin option (more direct, more elevation loss/regain): from Cascade Pass, drop east into Pelton Basin (established camp; reliable water at Doubtful Creek/Pelton Basin — fill up here, since Horseshoe Basin's own water is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk) and work cross-country toward the Black Warrior mine gully, a narrow (~8-ft-wide) rock dike dropping about 100 ft to the Horseshoe Basin side: Class 3 at the top, a short Class 4 downward step to an alcove with old mining equipment stashed in it, then continuing Class 3 but loose and exposed. From the basin floor (~6,600 ft) contour northeast then east on slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge below the summit notch. Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself, so most parties base at Sahale Glacier Camp or Pelton Basin and day-trip the peak from there — consistent with the ~16.8-mile (27 km) round-trip distance. Either way, expect extended travel on loose talus/scree and slabs with real fall exposure, a snow crossing that wants an axe (crampons in early season), and route-finding by cairn/climber's trail rather than maintained tread once past Sahale Arm or Pelton Basin.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the approach. From the base of the gully/ledge leading to Horseshoe's summit, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 to a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the true summit, exiting on a loose Class 3/4 ledge to the highpoint — a small, roughly one-meter-square notch atop Ripsaw Ridge. There is a solid rock horn on the east side of the notch that serves as the natural rappel anchor (parties also build a small gear anchor from a few cams if a horn sling is absent or worn). One rappel of roughly 100 ft (about 30 m) down the south-face ledge system returns you to the notch/gully below the summit: a 30 m rope reaches close to the bottom, with maybe the last 10 ft needing an easy downclimb, while a 60 m rope (doubled) or a single-strand 60 m lower reaches with rope to spare for a clean single rappel. There is no fixed/bolted hardware here — it's a natural horn and/or gear anchor, so carry a few cams as backup. From the base of the rappel, reverse whichever approach line was used: descend the loose gully/ledge back into Horseshoe Basin, re-cross the ~6,600-ft snowfield, and either regain Sahale Peak's ridge and the Sahale Arm Trail back to Cascade Pass, or climb back out of Pelton Basin over Cascade Pass to the trailhead. Loose, exposed rock on the summit ledges is the main descent hazard (helmet recommended, and manage rope carefully to avoid dislodging blocks); the long snow/scree/slab travel back to camp or the trailhead is otherwise straightforward but sustained.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward but long and with no shortcuts: reverse the Class 3 terrain to the saddle, then climb back out of Horseshoe Basin to Cascade Pass (or back over Sahale Arm) — there is no quick escape once you've dropped into the basin.

pitch_detail.notes: The full summit ramp climbed as one continuous roped pitch: begins as 3rd-class scrambling and steepens to 5.2 in the final section just below the top; belay/anchor at a horn on the summit.

itinerary.cal: Cascade River Road's June 2026 washout gate well below the Cascade Pass Trailhead has been lifted, and the park's road-conditions page, updated July 3, 2026, lists the road open — check nps.gov/noca road conditions again before you go, and pick up your Sahale Glacier/Horseshoe Basin camping permit at the Marblemount Ranger Station since sites can fill on summer weekends.

days.note: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead, climb switchbacks to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft, 3.7 mi) then continue up the Sahale Arm Trail to the permitted Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 ft. Most parties treat this as a half-day carry so they're fresh for an early alpine start the next morning.
days.title: Approach to Sahale Glacier Camp
days.objective: Reach Sahale Glacier Camp (7,600 ft) as base for the Horseshoe/Buckner traverse

days.note: Alpine start down off Sahale Arm into Horseshoe Basin, crossing snow/talus past old Davenport Mine relics to the base of Horseshoe's summit block. A short, exposed 5.2 step (rope, light rack, 30-60m) gains the true summit; most parties downclimb or make one short rappel back to the ledge. After returning to camp, break it down and hike the full ~5.7 mi / 4,000 ft back down to the trailhead the same day, making for a long but standard second day.

access.fees: $10/person + $6 reservation fee for overnight backcountry camping (2025 rate); day use/climbing with no overnight stay does not require a fee.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Camp only at designated/permitted sites (e.g., Sahale Glacier Camp, Pelton Basin) — this is a high-demand zone with an early-access lottery for peak season. Standard Leave No Trace / pack-out-waste rules apply; no campfires above treeline.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit required year-round; as of 2025 the fee is $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee (youth 15 and under free). Cascade River Road trailheads (Cascade Pass, Boston Basin, Eldorado) require in-person permit pickup at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount — advance Recreation.gov reservations must still be finalized there, or picked up walk-up (about 40% of sites are held for walk-ups).
access.closures: Cascade River Road was closed to vehicles at Eldorado (milepost 20) in June 2026 for flooding/landslide damage; that closure has been lifted, and the park's road-conditions page, updated July 3, 2026, lists the road open. Check the NPS road-conditions page and Skagit County road-closures page before heading out.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit — quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Parties starting from Stehekin can arrange the permit by email.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Open: the June 2026 closure to vehicles at Eldorado (milepost 20) for flooding/landslide damage has been lifted, and the park's road-conditions page, updated July 3, 2026, lists the road open.
road.driveNote: Gravel/paved, not suitable for sedans or low-clearance vehicles even when fully open; no RVs, large trailers, or vehicles over 22 ft. Road-end (Cascade Pass TH) sits at 3,660 ft, about 23 miles from Marblemount/Hwy 20.
road.seasonalGate: Typically opens to the Cascade Pass trailhead by late June each year (snowpack-dependent) and closes for the season with the first heavy snow.

climate.typical: Alpine, Cascade-crest climate: heavy snowpack lingers into July, the access road is often not fully open until late June, and afternoon convective thunderstorms are common in July-August. First snow can hit the high basins by mid-to-late September, quickly ending the practical season.

bySeason.fall: Possible into September in a dry year, but afternoon storms and the first snowfall can shut down access quickly; shorter daylight for the long approach.
bySeason.spring: Not viable until the road opens (typically late June) and the Cascade Pass Trail melts out; heavy, avalanche-prone snow persists lower down into early summer.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (mid-July-September): mostly snow-free but talus-heavy travel on Sahale Arm and through Horseshoe Basin; long exposed alpine walking with little shade.
bySeason.winter: Rarely attempted; the one documented winter ascent (Feb 2024) treated the SE face as an M3 mixed/ice route with full winter rack — not a scrambling objective.

emergency.notes: Horseshoe Peak sits directly on the Skagit/Chelan county line atop Ripsaw Ridge, so either county's SAR may be involved; NPS climbing rangers based in Marblemount typically coordinate backcountry rescues here, often by helicopter given the multi-mile approach. Cell coverage is unreliable to absent in Horseshoe Basin and on the ridge — carry a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) and leave your itinerary on your wilderness permit.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, Sedro-Woolley, WA — the closest ER to the Marblemount trailhead area (~25 mi via Hwy 20); Skagit Valley Hospital in Mount Vernon is a larger regional facility roughly 45 min further.

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July through August, often piggybacked on trips to Sahale Mountain, Boston Peak, or Horseshoe Basin camping
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - likely a handful of parties per season; The Mountaineers run occasional club 'Basic Alpine Climb' outings here, otherwise it sees mostly independent scramblers who are already in Boston Basin/Sahale Arm/Horseshoe Basin for other objectives

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong alpine fitness - approach via Sahale Arm/Boston Basin or Park Creek is a long, high-elevation-gain day (often split into a 2-day trip with a high camp) before the summit push
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Often carried as an overnight pack (camp gear, bivy) since most parties base out of Boston Basin or Horseshoe Basin rather than day-tripping

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 6-9 hours to a Boston Basin or Horseshoe Basin high camp, plus a separate summit day; feasible as a very long single push but typically done over 2 days
requiredSkills: Confident, careful movement on loose, exposed Class 3-4 rock
Route-finding off-trail across glaciated/snow approach terrain
Basic glacier-travel awareness and self-arrest for the approach
Self-sufficiency for a remote objective with long self-rescue distance
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate-to-advanced scrambler comfortable with sustained Class 3 and short exposed Class 4 moves well off-trail

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with late July-August as the most reliable stretch

July.reason: Route comes into season around mid-month as snow recedes on the saddle traverse; early July can still hold lingering snow on the approach

June.reason: Spring conditions mean the route is snow-covered with avalanche and glacier hazard - outside the season window

August.reason: Prime window - most stable weather and driest rock, though glaciers on approach are more broken late-season

September.reason: Still within season and generally stable, but days are shorter and early-season storms become possible

weather.typical: Alpine North Cascades weather; rapid changes possible
weather.probability: Afternoon convective buildups are common in the North Cascades in July-August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained Class 3 with a short, exposed Class 4 step and a narrow, low-prominence saddle traverse; a fall here, combined with the route's remote position and long self-rescue distance, raises the consequence well above a typical trade-route Class 3 scramble

avalanche.zone: No NWAC forecast zone covers this interior North Cascades NP location precisely; the nearest is East Slopes North

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Approach crosses glaciated terrain ('glaciated approach terrain'); most consequential earlier in season before it opens up and consolidates

sling_rack.runners: 2-3 slings for a hand line/short belay

backups.rope_note: Class 3 dike with a Class 4 down-step; published descriptions note it requires a little bit of roped climbing (half a pitch) — a short rope suffices.

approach_variants.name: Sahale Arm, the secret gully, and the mining-equipment alcove
approach_variants.notes: From Sahale Glacier Camp traverse the boulder-and-heather plateau east, downclimb the steep snowfield, and gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge; follow a cairned climbers' trail down it, past one short 4th-class step, descending easterly to about 7,100 ft. Pick up the southeast rib that forms the west edge of Horseshoe Basin and follow it southeast to the top of the so-called secret gully at about 6,700 ft — full of snow some years, completely melted out and loose in others. Below it, traverse a wide ledge at 6,600 ft rising gradually to the base of a cliff at 6,800 ft where old mining workings sit, then contour loose scree until you are due south of the peak. Fill up at Doubtful Creek or Pelton Basin: the water in Horseshoe Basin is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk.
hazards: Extended travel on loose talus, scree and slabs with real fall exposure
A snow crossing that wants an axe, and crampons in early season
Mine-tailings contamination of Horseshoe Basin water
Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: An alcove with old mining equipment stashed in it is the unmistakable marker. Dropping into Horseshoe Basin you use a narrow rock dike about eight feet wide that loses roughly a hundred feet: it starts Class 3, then a short downward Class 4 step lands you in that alcove with mining gear cached inside it, after which the dike stays Class 3 but loose and exposed. Nothing else on this ridge looks like it. Get the peak itself right before you commit: the crag climbers call Horseshoe is the highest point on Ripsaw Ridge, nearest Buckner, with the sharp Lick of Flame spire standing between the two. The twin-spired formation with a U-shaped notch in the middle of the ridge is the older, historical Horseshoe and is not the summit anyone bags — aiming at it puts you on the wrong tower. From the basin floor a snowfield at 30 to 45 degrees sits at the base of the peak and spills onto a large ledge about a hundred feet below the top; from there work leftward around a small buttress into the loose gully that leads to the notch just east of the summit, where the rope comes out for five feet of 5th class.

climbing_route.label: Snowfield and scree to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: From the stance in Horseshoe Basin, gain the snowfield at the base of the peak, then work left across scree and scramble easy blocky ground before dropping into a gully and following it up to the crest of the ridge linking Horseshoe with the Lick of Flame. Two variations of this section are described and both go at 3rd class; the terrain is loose throughout, so parties should stay off one another's fall line and avoid stacking up in the gully. Early in the season the snowfield at the base can be firm enough to want crampons as well as an axe.

climbing_route.label: Narrow summit ramp
climbing_route.notes: From the crest a narrow ramp leads up and climbers' left toward the summit. It begins as exposed 3rd-class ledge travel on scree-covered rock with a long drop below; the ramp is the only reasonable line to the top, and stepping off it puts you on steeper broken ground. Route-finding trap: the historical Horseshoe is the twin-spired formation with the U-shaped notch on Ripsaw Ridge, and neighbouring towers on the same ridge look plausible from below.

climbing_route.label: Summit step
climbing_route.notes: The ramp turns 5th class just under the top — a short steep move gains the roughly metre-square notch that is the summit. Reported as an easy Grade II, 5.2, usually climbed as a single pitch of about 100 ft; a 60 m rope and a light rack of cams protect it, with an anchor built at the base of the step. Aged webbing has been found on the summit and parties commonly make one single-rope rappel back down the ledge before reversing the scramble. This is a long day to carry a rope for a few metres of 5th class, but the exposure at the step is real and the rock is only moderately trustworthy.

bivy.name: Buckner cross-country zone bivy
bivy.notes: The option for climbers who want to sleep on the route rather than at a valley camp — high bivies on moraine, slab or snow under Buckner's north side and the Ripsaw Ridge peaks. Zone rules are strict and worth reading before you go: camp at least a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight, and only on snow, rock or bare ground. No meadow camping, nothing within 100 ft of water, no fires. Because the permit is walk-up only, a trip built around a zone bivy is one you cannot lock in ahead of time — carry a fallback.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent — snowmelt and seasonal streams in the upper basin, dependable early, thin or gone by late season
bivy.permit: NPS cross-country zone permit required, walk-up only. Buckner is not among the zones that take advance reservations, so it cannot be booked on Recreation.gov and must be picked up in person, generally no more than a day ahead.
bivy.capacity: 6 people per party, 6 parties per night in the zone

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: A set of hand-built rock-walled tent platforms at the toe of the glacier, at the top of Sahale Arm. It is high, exposed and above the last dependable water, so late-season parties should plan to melt snow or carry up from lower on the arm. For the Horseshoe Basin peaks it is a high camp rather than a basin camp — it serves approaches that cross Sahale Arm and drop toward Doubtful Lake and the head of the basin, and it puts you on the right side of the divide for Buckner's north aspect. Reported elevation varies slightly between sources.
bivy.water: Unreliable — snowmelt and glacier runoff only, and the seasonal trickles commonly dry up by late summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; one of the most contested designated camps in the park. Realistically needs the early-access lottery or the general on-sale window in late April.

bivy.name: Pelton Basin Camp
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

bivy.name: Basin Creek Camp
bivy.notes: The closest designated camp to the Horseshoe Basin trail junction, which sits at about 3,600 ft on the valley trail, so it is the practical base for anything up in the cirque. It has a separate cooking area, a bear box and its own privy. Capacity is tiny — three sites — so a party of four fills most of it and a weekend permit is not something to count on. From here the basin trail climbs roughly 1,300 ft in about 1.5 miles to the Black Warrior Mine and the waterfall headwall below Ripsaw Ridge and Buckner's north side.
bivy.water: Reliable — Basin Creek runs beside the camp all season
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA); designated camp reserved by site on Recreation.gov, with roughly 40% of inventory held for walk-up the day before at Marblemount or Golden West in Stehekin. Per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.

bivy.name: Doubtful Lake Camp
bivy.notes: Doubtful Lake lies in a cirque below Sahale Arm, reached by a spur that drops off the arm trail. It is the natural middle camp on the Sahale Arm variation of the approach, breaking up a long crossing between Cascade Pass and the head of Horseshoe Basin. Water is the one thing never in question here, which matters if the alternative is Sahale Glacier Camp late in the season. The spur loses meaningful elevation off the arm, so factor the reclimb into the next day.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus its inlet and outlet streams
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camping at the lake, reserved or walked up like the other Cascade Pass-area sites.
bivy.capacity: A small designated camp at the lake, site count not published. Treat it as a handful of spots rather than a place a large party can count on.

backups.name: East Slopes Scramble
backups.season: Nov-Apr (all documented ascents are winter/spring snowshoe or ski tours); dry-season scrambling conditions are not specifically documented for this peak
hazards: No maintained trail — expect real route-finding through brush low on the route
Loose rock, talus, and scree on the upper slopes
Wind-exposed, unshaded summit ridge
Lingering snow/ice on shaded sections into early summer
No reliable water source above the trailhead
backups.overview: Tye Peak (Pt. 5,476') is an unofficial name — it doesn't appear on USGS quads — for the summit rising directly above Stevens Pass on Skyline/Tye Ridge, between the Stevens Pass Ski Area and the Pacific Crest Trail corridor. The name comes from nearby Tye Lake and the Tye River. There's no maintained trail, and it draws little traffic, but its short approach from the highway makes it one of the fastest true summits in the corridor once the snow and brush clear.
backups.beta: From the Stevens Pass Ski Area, climb the service road/trail past Skyline Lake to a gap in Skyline Ridge, then descend the ridge's north/back side into a creek drainage before climbing back up to gain Tye Peak's south ridge, which leads to the summit. There is no maintained trail; the route is class 2 terrain but requires route-finding and, outside of firm snow cover, pushing through dense brush. Tye Peak and neighboring Sky Mountain share the same approach and are often combined in one trip.
backups.turnaround: Because the route crosses open avalanche terrain on Skyline Ridge's back side and has no trail for reliable route-finding, turn around if visibility drops, avalanche danger is considerable or higher on north-facing slopes, or the group's pace suggests a late, fatigued descent through brushy or icy terrain.
backups.face: South ridge, gained via a cross-country approach from the Skyline Lake basin (east side)
backups.descent: Reverse the east slopes back toward Stevens Pass.
obj_haz: Avalanche terrain on slopes flanking the approach and summit ridge
Whiteout/routefinding difficulty crossing the passes and drainage
Wet, rotten 'snice' surface conditions in spring

waypoints.name: Stevens Pass North Lot / Skyline Lake-PCT Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large day-use lot on the north side of US 2 at Stevens Pass summit; climbers' route starts on the gated service road just west of the PCT trailhead, beside the ski area's substation/utility building.
waypoints.directions: Drive US 2 to the Stevens Pass summit and park in the large day-use lot on the north side of the highway, signed for the PCT and Skyline Lake trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or Forest Service day-use fee applies here. The lot sits at about 4,060 feet, and the climbers' route leaves from the lot itself beside the ski area's substation and utility building, so there is no further driving once you are parked.

waypoints.name: Skyline Lake cutoff
waypoints.note: Service road passes a ski-area utility tower near 0.75 mi, then an easy-to-miss, cairn-marked left fork (about 1 mi in) leaves the road for Skyline Lake and the ridge; staying right leads to a cell tower instead.

waypoints.name: Skyline Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake reached via a short heather-and-huckleberry traverse off the service road; reliable water and a common rest stop/winter camp spot below Skyline Ridge.

waypoints.name: Skyline Ridge gap (steep drop-in)
waypoints.note: Crossing the low point in Skyline Ridge above the lake requires dropping a roughly 150-ft, ~50-degree slope on the back side; snow-free it's mossy, loose rock and brush underfoot, and in winter it can cornice — the route's real crux.

waypoints.name: Creek drainage below Skyline Ridge
waypoints.note: Route bottoms out at the head of a small creek on the north side of the ridge; early-season water source before the traverse toward Tye Ridge.

waypoints.name: Tye Ridge crest / heather benches
waypoints.note: Steep wooded slope opens into gentle snowy meadows near 4,900 ft, then climbs through thinning timber to gain the crest of Tye Ridge at ~5,000 ft — this is the open heather-bench terrain where the brush finally clears.

waypoints.name: Saddle between Sky Mountain and Tye Peak
waypoints.note: Estimated elevation for the connecting gap between Sky Mountain and Tye Peak's summit ridge; from here the route turns and climbs directly up the ridgeline to the top, staying on the highest ground to avoid cornices in winter or loose talus in summer.

waypoints.name: Tye Peak
waypoints.note: Broad, mostly open summit (aka Point 5476) with views of Rainier, Glacier Peak, Baring, and the Nason Ridge crest when clear; no register, no maintained trail — reverse the same line to descend.

Trekking poles for the steep, loose lower trail

One of the shortest true summits directly off US 2 — a good backup objective on a socked-in day when bigger Cascades goals are out.

backups.pro_needs: Non-technical class 2 scramble/snow climb — no rock rack is used. In firm, icy, or wind-scoured conditions on the Skyline Ridge slopes, some parties add lightweight crampons alongside an ice axe.
backups.best_season: Late July through September gives the driest brush and firmest footing on the upper slopes. Go earlier and you'll likely fight wet slide alder and residual snow patches on shaded ground; wait until October and the first crest snow can return. A separate winter/spring snow-climb or ski-touring line up the same general terrain exists (popular with Stevens Pass backcountry skiers), but it's a steeper, avalanche-exposed undertaking distinct from this summer scramble.
backups.approach: Park in the large day-use lot on the north side of US 2 right at the Stevens Pass summit (signed for the PCT/Skyline Lake trailhead); a Northwest Forest Pass or Forest Service day-use fee applies here. Leave from the east end of the lot near the ski area's substation and climb directly up the open east-facing slopes below Cowboy Mountain, or start on the Skyline Lake Trail a short distance to the west for a more established (if brushier) line.
backups.descent_text: Most parties descend the same east-slope line, watching footing carefully on loose talus and scree in the upper section. Some instead drop off the south ridge or the southeast-facing slopes back toward Skyline Ridge — scout the line before committing, since both options funnel into brush lower down. Lingering snow patches on shaded aspects can still be glissaded or plunge-stepped into early July.
backups.bail: Quick retreat to the pass is available throughout.

itinerary.cal: Most parties do this as a winter/spring snow climb from the ski area lot since the upper slopes are brushy class 2-3 bushwhacking in summer.

days.note: Start from the Stevens Pass Ski Area's north-side lot near the electrical substation, follow the ski-area access road/lift line up through the Skyline Lake/Skyline Ridge area, then pick up the east slopes to the summit ridge. There is no maintained trail above Skyline Ridge, so expect route-finding and some brush/scrambling in summer conditions (much cleaner as a snow climb in winter/spring). Reverse the same line to descend.

approach_variants.name: Skyline Lake and the ridge gap drop-in
approach_variants.notes: Start from the large day-use lot on the north side of the highway at the pass, beside the ski area's substation and utility building, on the gated service road. Around a mile in, an easy-to-miss cairn-marked left fork leaves the road for Skyline Lake and the ridge — staying right on the road takes you to a cell tower instead. Past the lake the route crosses the low point in Skyline Ridge, drops into a creek drainage on the ridge's back side, and climbs back out to gain the Tye Ridge crest. There is no maintained trail; snow-free this is a stiff bushwhack, which is why most ascents are made on continuous snow.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October, or on snow
hazards: A roughly 150-ft slope near fifty degrees on the back side of the ridge gap, which can cornice in winter
Mossy, loose rock and brush on that drop-in when snow-free
Dense brush low on the route once the snow melts out
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Wind-exposed summit ridge and no water above the creek drainage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route's crux is at its start, and the start goes down rather than up. From Skyline Lake climb northwest through timber to the low point in the crest of Skyline Ridge at about 5,200 ft. The far side is not a walk-through: it is a drop of roughly 150 feet at close to fifty degrees, mossy loose rock and brush when snow-free and liable to cornice in winter. That drop-in is the confirmation you are in the right gap — a gap you can simply stroll over is the wrong one, and there are several plausible low points along that crest. It bottoms out at the head of a small creek near 4,800 ft, an early-season water source and the last one. From there a steep wooded slope opens into gentle meadows around 4,900 ft and thins through timber to the crest of Tye Ridge near 5,000 ft, which is where the brush finally clears and the going turns to open heather benches. Follow the crest north to the saddle between Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, then climb the ridgeline directly, staying on the highest ground to avoid cornices in winter and loose talus in summer.

bivy.name: Skyline Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. Winter is the season here, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
bivy.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
bivy.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
bivy.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

backups.name: Improbable Traverse
backups.fa: Dave Hiser and Mike Borghoff, 1960; first winter ascent Kit Lewis, 1975
hazards: High objective rockfall danger: November 2021 rockfall event destroyed major section of route with 30x40ft section falling off
Traverse pitch now requires 5.9-5.10 downclimbing ~20 feet from old piton with 30+ feet of additional unprotected climbing
Very loose and crumbly rhyolite rock throughout route; poor rock quality except for traversing ledges
Intense afternoon sun exposure on west-facing wall intensifies rockfall danger and afternoon weather deterioration
Avalanche blasting from nearby Mount Snoqualmie ski resort in winter (contact 425-434-7669 for alerts)
backups.overview: A technical alpine rock climb on Guye Peak's prominent west face offering a classic 5.8 traverse pitch with stellar views from Interstate 90. Once popular, the route was heavily damaged by rockfall in November 2021; current conditions are marginal and downclimbing on the traverse is now required.
backups.beta: Start from Alpental parking lot and hike up talus cone via Ober Strasse Road (controversial private access; use new non-established approach avoiding private roads as of 2021). Scramble ~200 feet of loose, mossy, dirty slabs to reach first anchor. Climb 6 pitches of mixed alpine rock through crumbly terrain to Lunch Ledge at ~300 feet. The iconic traverse (pitches 4-5) traverses right on good ledges with old fixed pitons; now requires careful downclimbing due to 2021 damage. Upper pitches climb Class 4 ramp terrain with trees and exposure to summit. Route is sustained and exposed throughout; not a beginner alpine rock climb.
backups.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround time before starting the technical pitches that leaves a comfortable margin to finish the descent in daylight — afternoon thunderstorms and the loose rock make climbing in fading light or wet conditions considerably more hazardous here.
backups.alpine_grade: III 5.8 (Mountaineers list the outing as II 5.8 plus scrambling)
backups.rappels: No rappels on the climb itself. The descent over the summits requires one ~30 m rappel from a slung tree on the east side below the middle summit into the SE couloir; parties who lose the line or get benighted have reported using up to four tree rappels. Carry a 60 m rope, extra webbing and rap rings.
backups.comms: Cell phone service generally available at Alpental parking area (AT&T, Verizon coverage). No reliable service on route itself. Contact Mount Snoqualmie ski resort at 425-434-7669 for avalanche conditions and ski resort operations status.
backups.descent: Traverse north over subsummits with climbers' trail; descent varies seasonally. Alternative: rappel from tree anchors on east side of summit to bypass exposed terrain and avoid reverse-traversing dangerous sections. Some descend via Southeast Couloir toward Cave Ridge and Snow Lake trail.
obj_haz: avalanche-control blasting from Alpental in winter/spring

backups.detailed_rack: Mid-size alpine rock rack with 6-8 cams and nuts (mostly cams for Guye's crumbly rock); 60-meter rope minimum (bring two ropes for safe rappel options); full rack of medium to large chocks; several double runners or slings for extending placements around flakes; helmet (mandatory); climbing shoes; approach shoes or boots.
what_to_bring: Water (minimum 2-3L due to altitude and exposure)
Headlamp (long approach in summer daylight, but plan for changes)
pro_tips: The iconic traverse pitch (5.8) is the crux with good ledges for feet and several old fixed pitons providing protection
Lunch Ledge at ~300 feet provides good rest/belay ledge before committing to upper pitches
Watch for extremely loose sections throughout; much of route is crumbly and unstable
Use slings to extend placements around flakes and poor rock
Start early to finish before afternoon sun intensity and weather changes
November 2021 rockfall significantly damaged the route—many parties now recommend descending via alternatives
watch_out: Rockfall danger is extreme and increasing due to November 2021 damage; route condition is marginal and getting worse
Traverse pitch now involves exposed 5.9-5.10 downclimbing with inadequate protection—many consider it not recommended
Loose rock and dirt throughout; expect to encounter unstable blocks and flakes requiring careful footwork
High consequence scrambling on approach and upper pitches
Afternoon wind, sun, and storm development rapid in July-September
backups.pro_needs: Protection is generally intermittent and poor-quality due to loose flakes and crumbly rock. Many dirt-filled cracks yield marginal placements. Several old fixed pitons remain on the traverse pitch itself. Plan for lots of sling extensions around features rather than clean gear placements. Tree anchors available for rappel.
backups.best_season: June through October offer best alpine rock climbing conditions at Guye Peak. July-September provide most stable weather and driest conditions. Avoid winter due to avalanche danger, heavy snow, and rockfall hazards. Spring (April-May) has variable conditions with lingering snow.
backups.approach: From Alpental Ski Area parking lot (3,120 ft), walk through residential area on Ober Strasse Road to talus cone base beneath west face (note: as of 2021, private road access is contested; climbers must use new non-established approach avoiding Alpental Community Club private roads). Approach time ~30 minutes to 1 hour from parking.
backups.descent_text: After summiting via Improbable Traverse, most climbers traverse north over Guye's north and middle summits to descend via established gully systems. A climbers' trail descends from the Guye-Snoqualmie saddle area. For faster/safer descent, fixed anchors (tree with rap tatters) provide rappel opportunity on east side of summit to bypass exposure. Southeast Couloir descent toward Cave Ridge parking is viable alternative.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward from the lower pitches by downclimbing or building a gear/tree anchor before committing to the traverse; above the traverse, especially through the post-2021 rockfall damage, retreat is difficult and the party should be prepared to continue rather than reverse the crux.

pitch_detail.notes: Initial low to mid-5th class climbing through loose, crumbly rhyolite terrain; lots of holds but quality poor and exposed
Continuation of crumbly terrain leading toward Lunch Ledge; climbers should carefully test all holds
Final approach to Lunch Ledge (~300 ft from start); large comfortable belay ledge provides good rest point before upper pitches

The iconic Improbable Traverse pitch(es): traverse right on good foot ledges with several old fixed pitons for protection. Critical: November 2021 rockfall destroyed ~30x40ft section; now requires downclimbing 5.9-5.10 from old pin with 30+ feet of unprotected traversing. Many now recommend this route is not safe.
Class 4 ramp climbing through alpine trees and rock slabs to summit ridge approach; short but exposed

backups.itinerary: Single-day car-to-car outing from Seattle. Leave the city by 4:30-5:00 am, park at Alpental, be scrambling the talus cone by first light, aim to be starting the roped climbing within an hour of leaving the car. Expect roughly 5-7 hours on the route depending on how much you simulclimb, then 2.5-4 hours to get over the three summits and down the Cave Ridge bootpath. Published trip reports range from about 8 hours for a fast, competent pair to 14+ hours for a party that pitches everything out - one well-known report started at 10:30 am and exited at 1 am. There is no reason to camp; if you want a relaxed day, camp at a Snoqualmie Pass area campground the night before rather than on the mountain.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to September, when the talus approach is snow-free and the loose west face is at its driest

May.reason: Snow lingers on the talus cone and the stream bed at its end runs with meltwater, and freeze-thaw keeps loosening the crumbly rhyolite.

July.reason: Dry rock and long days; the west face bakes in afternoon sun, so an early start avoids heat and rockfall loosened by warming.

June.reason: The talus approach melts out and the face dries between storms, though the stream bed and mossy lower slabs can still be wet.

August.reason: Driest rock of the year and the stream bed is often dry; climb in the morning before the west face heats up, and watch for wildfire smoke.

October.reason: Fall rain soaks the dirty, mossy slabs and loose ledges, days are short, and early snow can reach the talus field below the face.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures on the sunny west face and stable weather, with dry rock and less afternoon heat.

approach_variants.name: Talus cone below the west face
approach_variants.notes:
Same problem and same ground as the rest of the west face. The roads named 'Strasse' off the Alpental access road are private; since 2021 the Alpental Community Club has forbidden both driving and walking on them, and climbers have been confronted by residents. The talus field has to be reached by a line that avoids private land, and no established path exists.

The route begins at the top of the talus cone below the face. Reckon on roughly half an hour to an hour from wherever you park to the top of the cone, and wear a helmet on the talus.
hazards: no established approach to the talus - the historic approach crosses private roads residents forbid
loose mossy slab scrambled unroped above the talus
a snow cone at the base of the slabs in early season
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus cone
poor rock quality on all but the traverse pitch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the top of the talus, a couple of hundred feet of loose, mossy, dirty slab is scrambled to reach the roped climbing; in early season a small snow cone sits at the bottom of those slabs and parties have used a nut tool as a self-belay across it. None of that is the route — the route starts where the scrambling ends.

The sequence that confirms you are on it: pitch one wanders about 100 ft of low fourth to low fifth to a tree belay; pitch two runs another 100 ft to a slung block; pitch three arrives at a large terrace known as Lunch Ledge. If three pitches have gone by and you have not reached an obviously large ledge, you are not on the line.

The named traverse pitch is well above Lunch Ledge. Everything below it is poor, loose rock, so bad rock low down does not mean you are lost — it is the one pitch of good rock that is the exception here, not the rule.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

backups.overview: Kololo Peaks is a sprawling, multi-summit massif on the southern flank of the Glacier Peak (DaKobed) massif, about 3 miles south of Glacier Peak itself. It has been called 'almost a nunatak' because it is nearly surrounded by ice - the White Chuck and Suiattle Glaciers flank it to the west/north and the Honeycomb and White River Glaciers to the east/south. It's a Class 2-3 snow/glacier objective, not technically hard, but the combination of a 12+ mile approach (much of it off-trail), extensive glacier travel, and remote route-finding make it a serious undertaking reserved for parties with solid glacier-travel and navigation skills.
backups.beta: Kololo Peaks presents three viable multi-day approaches, all exceeding 12 miles and typically requiring 2-3 days with glacier travel. The standard route from the west via North Fork Sauk Trail offers the most established access, climbing through old-growth forest to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, then traversing multiple glacier systems. The climb itself is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on talus and snow, with the primary challenge being glacier crevasse navigation and length of approach rather than technical difficulty. Neither summit presents hard climbing; the route involves walking across easy terrain between the west summit and the slightly higher east summit (8,240 ft, the true high point).
backups.turnaround: Firm turnaround given the remote, snowy approach
backups.rappels: None typically needed — descent reverses the ascent route
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.comms: Zero cell service in Glacier Peak Wilderness. Satellite communicator (Garmin InReach, Spot) strongly recommended for emergency notification.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent line: descend the low-angle ice sheet/rock scramble back onto the glacier, then re-cross the White Chuck (or White River) Glacier's crevasse bands roped up to return to high camp, and retrace the approach trail (White Pass/North Fork Sauk, or Lightning Creek/White River) back to the trailhead. No rappels are typically required on the standard route.
obj_haz: whiteout/weather exposure on open glacier plateau

waypoints.name: North Fork Sauk Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 49 (6.4 mi off the Mountain Loop Hwy area); Northwest Forest Pass required and a self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk; start of North Fork Sauk Trail #649.

waypoints.name: Pilot Ridge Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail #649 forks with Pilot Ridge Trail #652 here; stay on #649 (the lower, riverside route) toward Mackinaw Shelter.
waypoints.directions: The first two miles are the gentlest of the trip: an easy grade through old-growth forest along the North Fork Sauk River, gaining only a few hundred feet.

waypoints.name: Red Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Red Creek on the climbers' path; hikers describe it as 'interesting but not difficult' at normal flow, tougher during peak snowmelt.
waypoints.directions: Two more nearly flat miles up the valley on good tread, crossing several small tributaries on the way. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you — it is manageable at normal flow but runs considerably higher during snowmelt or after heavy rain, and a pole or a sturdy stick helps with balance.

waypoints.name: Mackinaw Shelter
waypoints.note: Historic three-sided log shelter beside the North Fork Sauk River; the last easy, reliable camp before the trail turns steep and switchbacked toward White Pass.
waypoints.directions: A last easy mile beside the river brings you to the shelter clearing. Flat ground here is limited and a larger party will find it tight. Fill water before moving on, because the trail leaves the river from this point.

waypoints.name: White Pass (PCT junction)
waypoints.note: Trail #649 tops out on the Pacific Crest Trail after ~3.2 steep miles from Mackinaw Shelter; broad meadow/basin here with camping and a view down into Foam Basin.
waypoints.directions: The trail turns uphill in earnest and gains roughly 3,000 ft in sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail, where Glacier Peak and the White Chuck side of the massif first come into view. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to the pass. This is the last easy, reliable water before the high traverse.

waypoints.name: Glacier Gap crevasse crossing
waypoints.note: Crossing point between the White Chuck Glacier and White River Glacier near a tarn-dotted basin; crevasses open by late season here — rope up before continuing toward Kololo.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows, the usual base camp, either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. From camp climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier to the gap — this is glacier travel on largely featureless snow, so carry a track or the navigation skill to retrace it in cloud, and be roped for the crevasses low on the glacier, which can be fully open.

waypoints.name: Kololo Peaks (summit)
waypoints.note: Summit gained by a short rock scramble off the White River Glacier after the final low-angle ice/snow pitch; of the twin tops a short walk apart, the eastern one is the true high point by 10-15 ft, so tag both.
waypoints.directions: From the gap gain the flat shoulder at about 6,000 ft, then follow the connecting ridge north-northwest over a bulge near 7,200 ft, cross the small basin below the east summit, and continue west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. From the saddle, the ridge forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque leads to the final low-angle snow and a short talus-and-ledge scramble to the top. Expect a stretch of exposed blue ice a couple of hundred yards long on the White River Glacier — that section wants crampons and deliberate footwork rather than a plod.

backups.detailed_rack: Ice axe, crampons, climbing harness, 30m+ glacier travel rope, crevasse rescue kit (2 prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, pulley, locking carabiners), helmet, glacier glasses and sunscreen (high UV/reflectivity on open snow), trekking poles for the long approach. Group gear: detailed map/compass or GPS with route track, water filter/treatment, and standard overnight camping gear for the 2-3 day trip.
what_to_bring: Water filter or treatment (no potable water at high camp)
GPS with a pre-loaded route track, or detailed map and compass
Satellite communicator (InReach/spot) - no cell coverage in the wilderness interior
Rain shell - weather changes quickly even in mid-summer
pro_tips: Bring a GPS track or very detailed map/compass skills - the trail beyond Foam Basin (west route) or beyond Lightning Creek (east route) disappears, and glacier navigation on featureless snow is easy to get wrong
Carry a water filter; there's no running water at either standard high camp beyond glacier melt
Set a firm turnaround time on the glacier crossing - afternoon cloud buildup or whiteout on the open ice makes retracing your route back to camp much harder
Verify road and trailhead status before you drive out - FR 49 has repeated washouts and the whole west approach has been cut off by Mountain Loop Highway landslides
watch_out: Extensive unmarked, off-trail travel demands real map/compass or GPS navigation skill, not just trail-following
Crevasses open up and become harder to read as the season progresses (worse Aug-Sept) - rope up and carry full crevasse-rescue gear
No reliable water at high camp beyond glacier/snow melt - carry a filter
This is a long way from help - self-rescue capability and a filed trip plan are essential
Check current road/trail alerts before driving out; FR 49 and the Mountain Loop Highway have a history of washouts and closures
backups.pro_needs: Glacier/snow protection where present; minimal rock pro
backups.best_season: Late July through September. Earlier in the season the approach and glacier are more continuously snow-covered, which can ease travel but adds avalanche and creek-crossing hazard (Red Creek/Lightning Creek run high with snowmelt); by August-September glaciers open up with more visible (and more hidden) crevasses, and in late summer/early fall the White Chuck side can sometimes be climbed with little or no true glacier travel.
backups.approach: The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which parties describe as interesting but not difficult to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the glacier, gain the flat shoulder at ~6,000 ft, then climb the connecting ridge NNW to a bulge at 7,200 ft, cross a small basin below Kololo's east summit, and continue west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft, from which the ridge forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque leads to the final glacier/talus/ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the round trip runs roughly 28-30 miles — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line.
backups.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line rather than following a separate down-route: downclimb the summit talus/ledges and upper glacier back to the 7,400 ft saddle, follow the connecting ridge back down to the ~6,000 ft shoulder, and re-cross the White River Glacier, Glacier Gap, and White Chuck Glacier back to Foam Basin/White River Meadows camp, then retrace the boot path over White Pass to the PCT/North Fork Sauk Trail junction and down the switchbacks and river-valley trail miles to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are known on this route, and parties describe reversing the glacier-and-ridge line rather than any rope-lowering. The real descent hazards are glacier hazards, not rock hazards: one party found fully open crevasses low on the White Chuck Glacier requiring careful route-finding/crampon work, and a roughly 200-yard section of exposed blue ice (a shallow icefall) on the White River Glacier that demands careful crampon travel; stay roped for glacier travel on the way down as well as up, and expect snow bridges to be less trustworthy and crevasses less obvious in early season than by late summer. Budget real time for the descent — the same party took about 5.3 hours from summit back to camp alone, before the multi-hour trail hike-out. Glissading may be feasible on snow-filled sections below the shoulder for parties comfortable self-arresting, especially early season, but it is an optional shortcut, not a required part of the route.
backups.bail: There are no fixed bail/rappel stations on this snow-and-glacier route - if conditions turn, simply reverse your tracks back across the glacier to camp. The real bail decision point is timing: turn around early enough to avoid crossing the open, featureless glacier in a whiteout or afternoon thunderstorm.

pitch_detail.notes: White River Trail #1507 (or North Fork Sauk Trail #649 on the west side) for roughly 10-12 miles to the point you leave maintained trail.
Off-trail travel up open slopes and talus to the flat shoulder near 6,000 ft on the south ridge (or to White River Meadows/Foam Basin on the west-side variant).
Roped travel across the upper White River Glacier (or White Chuck Glacier via Glacier Gap on the west variant), negotiating crevasses and, late season, a shallow icefall.
Scramble talus and ledges to the true summit; Kololo Peaks has twin summits a short scramble apart, and the eastern one is the true high point by 10-15 ft.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed July-September once the North Fork Sauk trail, White Pass, and Foam Pass are snow-free enough for travel and glacier crevasses have opened up; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the trailhead and the route lies in the Glacier Peak Wilderness.

days.note: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,080 ft), follow the North Fork Sauk Trail past Red Creek and the old Mackinaw Shelter site, then climb steeply (about 3,000 ft in 4 miles) to White Pass (5,900 ft). Continue over Foam Pass and drop into the White Chuck River basin, camping near Lake 6433 at roughly 6,700 ft. This is the longest, most grinding day of the trip.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, ~28-30 mile round trip with roughly 9,500 ft of cumulative gain/loss: one long approach day to a ~6,700 ft glacier-basin camp, an alpine-start summit day (9-10 hrs round trip) crossing the White Chuck and White River Glaciers, and a hike back out.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/annual Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent Interagency Pass) required for parking at both the North Fork Sauk and White River trailheads
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) inside Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft in wilderness.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead before entering Glacier Peak Wilderness (available at both the North Fork Sauk and White River/Indian Creek trailheads)
access.closures: A landslide closed the Mountain Loop Highway at milepost 37.5 (~15.5 mi south of Darrington) from December 2025, blocking vehicle access to FR 49 and the North Fork Sauk/Sloan Creek trailheads; repairs reopened the highway in mid-May 2026. Check Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before planning the west approach. Even when open, FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) has rough washout sections near miles 1 and 6; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (west/North Fork Sauk approach) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (east/White River approach) - both within Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

overnight_permit.where: Sign the trailhead register; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at most of these trailheads.

road.name: Forest Road 49 (Sloan Creek Road) via Mountain Loop Highway
road.status: Open — the Mountain Loop Highway landslide at MP 37.5 that blocked FR 49 and the North Fork Sauk Trailhead from December 2025 was repaired and the highway reopened in mid-May 2026; verify current status before driving
road.driveNote: From Darrington, follow the Mountain Loop Highway ~19.7 mi along the west side of the Sauk River, then turn onto Sloan Creek Road (FR 49) and continue ~6.6 mi to North Fork Sauk Trailhead. FR 49 is rough with washouts near miles 1 and 6 even in a normal year - high-clearance vehicle recommended.

climate.typical: West of the Cascade crest, the Glacier Peak Wilderness gets heavy precipitation and rapidly changing mountain weather even in summer - parties often report rain on the hike in and/or out despite climbing in July-September. Reliable snow-free travel on the approach trails generally isn't consistent until mid-to-late July; afternoon cloud buildup and showers are common through the season.

emergency.notes: No reliable cell coverage inside the Glacier Peak Wilderness - carry a satellite communicator (InReach/spot) and file a trip plan given the remote, multi-day, largely off-trail nature of this climb.
emergency.county: Straddles Snohomish County (west/North Fork Sauk approach) and Chelan County (east/White River approach)
emergency.rangerStation: Darrington Ranger District, (360) 436-1155 (west approach); Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth, (509) 548-2550 (east approach)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Valley Hospital, Arlington WA (Level IV ED) via the west/Darrington approach; Central Washington Hospital, Wenatchee WA or Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth WA via the east/White River approach

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July through August weekends, largely driven by club-scheduled trips
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Roughly 10-25 parties per season — a handful of scheduled Seattle Mountaineers Basic Glacier/Alpine Climb outings plus independent experienced parties; not a high-traffic objective

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very strenuous; multi-day approach on the order of 12+ miles one-way (up to ~29 miles round trip via White Pass) with major elevation gain/loss to reach a high camp before the summit push
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy overnight/glacier-camping load (tent, glacier travel gear, several days of food/fuel) — roughly 35-45 lbs

partner_requirements.approachTime: 1-2 days to high camp (12+ miles one-way via North Fork Sauk / White River or White Pass approaches); typically climbed as a 2-3 day trip, not a day trip
requiredSkills: Glacier travel and crevasse rescue (roped travel, self/team rescue)
Ice axe and crampon proficiency on snow/glacier terrain
Off-trail route-finding and navigation over long, remote approaches
Backcountry/glacier camping competence for a multi-day trip
High level of physical conditioning for sustained long days
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climber/scrambler — the terrain itself is only Class 2-3, but the extreme remoteness, long multi-day approach, and glacier travel make this unsuitable for beginners

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, tapering into early September before fall storms arrive

July.reason: Approach trails and glacier may still hold significant early-season snow; snow bridges over crevasses are less reliable/visible early in the month, adding glacier hazard even though access is opening up

August.reason: Best combination of snow coverage and stability this is the best window, though snow can still linger high into mid-summer in a heavy year

September.reason: Crevasses typically open and easily seen/avoided with less glacier hazard, but shortening days and possible early storms reduce the margin for a long remote day

weather.typical: Heavy North Cascades maritime snowpack with glaciers/lingering snow into summer
weather.probability: Early fall storms can arrive by September; summer afternoon thunderstorms are possible in the North Cascades though not specifically documented for this peak

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 2-3 scrambling near the summits with loose rock; the greater consequence driver is the sheer remoteness and length of the approach — a slip, injury, or weather change far from any road access is a serious self-rescue problem in extreme remoteness

avalanche.zone: Approximate NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (covers the North Cascades/Glacier Peak Wilderness area), but NWAC does not issue forecasts during the July-September climbing season, so no route-specific in-season avalanche rating exists

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Real hazard on the Suiattle/White Chuck Glacier crossing en route to the peaks; more concealed and dangerous early season when snow bridges are intact, more visible and avoidable by late summer/early fall as about 'snowfields and possible glacier travel on the Glacier Peak massif flanks'

gaps: No precise season-wide party-count or crowd data was found; the estimate is inferred from the presence of scheduled Mountaineers club trips and the remote, long-approach nature of the route
No NWAC or other forecast zone specifically covers Kololo Peaks in-season (avalanche forecasting there is a winter/spring product, not issued during the July-September climbing window)

Exact glacier/crevasse conditions vary significantly year to year (the White Chuck Glacier has notably diminished in recent years per trip reports) and were not independently re-verified beyond the on-file data and general trip-report descriptions
No specific documented afternoon-thunderstorm frequency data for this exact peak
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.
