approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
camps: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt — the first is an ordinary ford at normal flow and a stopper at high water
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last several off any maintained trail, so a navigation error is measured in hours
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier that are unreadable under early-season cover
Road closures on FR-49 and the Mountain Loop Highway that can shut the west approach entirely, turning this into a much longer trip from the east
approach_variants.baseFinding: This route has two arrivals and they are different kinds of thing. The first is where glacier travel starts, and the second is where the scrambling starts. Confusing them is how a party ends up unroped in the wrong place. Glacier starts at foam pass. From camp climb to Foam Pass and step onto the White Chuck Glacier. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure. Scrambling starts at the 7,400 ft saddle, and you get there by counting rather than by looking. Off the glacier, gain the flat shoulder near 6,000 ft; follow the connecting ridge north-north-west over a bulge at 7,200 ft; cross the small basin below the east summit; then go west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. Shoulder, bulge, basin, saddle — four things in that order. If you have gone west without first crossing a basin, you are on the wrong side of the bulge. The arrival test at the saddle: from it, one ridge runs away from you forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque. That ridge is the route. If the ground ahead does not have a glacier cirque falling away on one side of it, you are not on the saddle you want. What too far looks like: continuing east instead of west from the 7,200 ft bulge takes you to the east summit rather than the summit ridge — and of the twin tops on the summit ridge the eastern one is the true high point by only 10-15 ft, so bag both. One thing to expect on the ice rather than look for: a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice, a shallow icefall, on the White River Glacier. It is a crampon problem, not a navigation one, but it is the reason the descent takes longer than the map suggests.

approach_variants.name: White River trail from the east
approach_variants.notes: From the White River trailhead beyond Lake Wenatchee, walk the White River trail about 10 miles up the valley to the Lightning Creek crossing, then go cross-country up into the high basin east of the peaks. About as far on foot as the Sauk side, with less trail and more off-trail travel.

climbing_route.label: White Chuck Glacier to the White River Glacier
climbing_route.notes: From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier. This is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges.

climbing_route.label: Connecting ridge NNW to the 7,400 ft saddle
climbing_route.notes: From the glacier, gain the flat shoulder at ~6,000 ft, then climb the connecting ridge NNW to a bulge at 7,200 ft, cross a small basin below Kololo's east summit, and continue west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft.

climbing_route.label: Cirque-edge ridge and summit scramble
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle the ridge forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque leads to the final glacier/talus/ledge scramble to the summit.

bivy.name: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
bivy.notes: The climbing camp for Kololo Peaks, and the reason Kololo is a three-day trip rather than a weekend scramble. It sits in the stark rock-and-snow basin on the edge of what remains of the White Chuck Glacier, reached from the North Fork Sauk road end by twelve or thirteen miles of walking — the long river approach, then the steep switchbacking climb to White Pass, then east on the crest trail and out along the Foam Basin path toward Foam Pass. Eight hours from the road to camp is a normal rather than a slow time for a party carrying overnight gear. From here the peaks themselves are straightforward, a walk on glacier remnant and snow followed by easy scrambling on rubbly volcanic rock, and moving from one summit to the next is simple. The glacier is the thing to understand: it has retreated further and faster than almost anything in the range and much of what maps show as ice is now bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds, with the surviving ice thin, hard and holed by open crevasses late in the season. That means crampons rather than a snow plod by September, and it means route descriptions written twenty years ago describe a surface that is gone. Lower camps on the same approach sit at the river bench, at White Pass and at the gap above this basin. Exposed ground with no shelter, confusing in fog, and a long way from help.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams and ponds through the basin, running all through the climbing season and often silty. Late in a hot summer the flow drops to a trickle off the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time. Everybody camped here drinks it, so site the toilet well away from it.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free self-issue permit collected at the North Fork Sauk trailhead box, twelve-person party limit. No fires: this is bare rock, pumice and snow above treeline with nothing to burn and nothing that recovers. Human waste is carried out or buried properly well away from the meltwater. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
bivy.capacity: Open bare-ground bivouac sites scattered through the basin, with room for several parties and no crowding — this is a big, empty place. Rock-walled windbreaks left by previous parties are the nearest thing to a built site.

bivy.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
bivy.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. Painted mountain, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a day objective with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. Kololo Peaks is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
bivy.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
bivy.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside Glacier Peak Wilderness, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

backups.name: West Ridge
gear: Rope for the optional rappel near the summit
A few slings for the rappel anchor
hazards: Loose, crumbly schist/marble rock across the whole route.
A short but exposed Class 4 step just below the summit.
backups.overview: The peak's standard/easiest line: climbs the crest of Martin Peak's west ridge from Holden Pass to the summit, mostly Class 3 scrambling on loose schist with one short, well-featured Class 4 step just below the top.
backups.beta: From Holden Pass (the saddle shared with Bonanza Peak), gain the ridge via a series of gullies, scrambling on the right (south) side of the crest and repeating this pattern upward. The rock is loose/crumbly throughout, so route-finding by cairn is common. A short, exposed Class 4 section with good holds is encountered just below the summit; a fixed rappel anchor has been observed there for parties who prefer to rope up rather than downclimb it.
backups.turnaround: As with any loose, exposed North Cascades scramble, set a firm turnaround time that gets you off summit/ridge terrain before afternoon thunderstorms build and leaves a comfortable daylight margin for the slow, loose descent — don't push for the summit if you're not moving at your planned pace.
backups.rappels: One short optional rappel off a fixed anchor observed near the summit, past the crux Class 4 step; some parties downclimb this section instead.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.descent: Downclimb (or partly rappel) the same west-ridge line back to Holden Pass.
obj_haz: Short but real exposure on the Class 4 summit step

backups.detailed_rack: A single 30-60m rope with a light rack — a handful of small-to-mid cams/nuts and a few slings — is enough to protect the roped Class 3-4 sections and the exposed Class 4 crux gully below the summit. Many strong scrambling parties climb the route unroped in dry conditions; a helmet is recommended given the loose rock.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (early-season snow near Holden Pass)
Trekking poles for the scree/gully sections
pro_tips: A fixed rappel anchor near the summit lets you avoid downclimbing the exposed Class 4 crux.
Follow cairns through the loose gully sections on both ascent and descent — it's easy to wander onto worse rock without them.
watch_out: The schist rock is loose and crumbly along the entire ridge — test holds carefully.
The Class 4 step below the summit has real exposure despite generally good holds.
backups.pro_needs: Most parties travel unroped; a rope and a few slings/a picket cover the single optional rappel near the summit for those who don't want to downclimb the Class 4 step.
backups.approach: All approaches to Martin Peak begin at Holden Village: take the Lake Chelan ferry (Chelan Boat Company's Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express) from Chelan or Fields Point Landing to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up an 11-mile gravel road (12 switchbacks) into Holden Village. From Holden, follow the Railroad Creek Trail up-valley and continue to Holden Pass, the saddle between Bonanza and Martin Peaks, to reach the base of the west ridge.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line down the west ridge, following cairns back through the loose gully sections. The fixed rappel anchor near the summit allows a short rappel past the crux Class 4 step for parties who don't want to downclimb it; the rest of the descent is downclimbed. Expect the same loose-rock hazard on the way down as on the way up.
backups.bail: Retreat by downclimbing the ridge/gully line back toward Holden Pass; the crux gully just below the summit has a fixed rappel anchor as an alternative to downclimbing it.

pitch_detail.notes: Holden Pass to the base of the west ridge; talus/scramble to gain the ridge crest.
Ridge crest scramble easterly; easier terrain lies on climber's right (south side) of the crest, through ribs and a loose, beige-marble gully.
About 100 ft below the summit: a steep, exposed summit gully — the route's crux. A fixed rappel anchor is present nearby.

itinerary.cal: Lady of the Lake ferry to Lucerne runs a limited schedule and should be reserved in advance; confirm the return sailing time before setting a fixed exit day.

days.note: Catch the Lady of the Lake ferry from Field's Point to Lucerne, then the Holden Village shuttle, before hiking the Railroad Creek / Holden Pass trail up to camp at ~6,400 ft. The trail is in good shape and shared by Bonanza-bound parties, so Holden Pass is a well-established camp spot with water nearby.

days.note: From Holden Pass, traverse east along the ridge linking Bonanza to Martin to the saddle at the foot of the West Ridge, then cut right onto the south side of the ridge into a loose scree gully. Climb the gully and exit via a short Class 3-4 rock step near its top just below an overhang, then keep linking gullies on the south side of the crest up to the summit block. The rock is notoriously loose ("choss"), so a helmet and careful route-finding through the exit moves matter more than raw fitness.

road.name: Holden Village Road (Lucerne Landing to Holden Village)
road.status: Closed to vehicles and hikers since January 2026 after December 2025 flood and landslide damage (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-05-26-04, in effect through December 31, 2027 unless rescinded sooner); the Lucerne dock is closed too, so do not plan to enter or leave through Lucerne or Holden. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also covers FR 8301 and the Lower Railroad Creek Trail through October 31, 2026. Check with the Chelan Ranger District, (509) 682-4900, before you go. road.driveNote: There is no drive-in trailhead. Ferry to Lucerne Landing, then an 11-mile gravel road with 12 switchbacks by Holden Village shuttle bus to reach Holden Village and the Railroad Creek Trail.

climate.typical: Climbed almost exclusively July-September once seasonal snow clears from the approach gullies. The Railroad Creek valley at Holden Village (3,200 ft) is warm and buggy in early-mid summer, while the exposed upper ridge and gully can hold hard snow/ice into July in above-average years. Afternoon thunderstorms are the main summer hazard on the loose, exposed upper ridge.

bySeason.fall: Possible into September, but ferry/shuttle service tapers off in October and early storms can put fresh snow on the already-loose rock.
bySeason.summer: Prime window; August is generally most reliable for snow-free rock. Expect black flies (3,000-4,000 ft) and mosquitoes near Holden Lake.

emergency.notes: Very remote wilderness area with no road access — reached only by Lake Chelan ferry to Lucerne plus an 11-mile shuttle road/trail into Holden Village. Plan on unreliable cell coverage and a long, boat-dependent evacuation timeline.
emergency.rangerStation: Chelan Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest

crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic; likely well under 20 parties/season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, sustained hiking fitness for a long approach from Holden Lake/Hart Lake basins with significant elevation gain over talus and heather benches
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (camp gear, several days of food) given remote Chelan-ferry access to Holden

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long, committing multi-day approach (ferry/shuttle to Holden Village, then trail and cross-country travel to Holden or Hart Lake basins before the climb)
requiredSkills: off-trail routefinding through talus and heather benches
wilderness self-sufficiency (no cell coverage, boat-only egress)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced off-trail scrambler comfortable with unmarked wilderness travel and loose talus; boat-only, multi-day approach demands self-sufficiency and good judgment far from rescue

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August is the core window; late July through September is climbable but shoulder months carry more snow/weather risk

July.reason: Late July can still hold lingering snow on the approach and slopes; talus may be snow-covered early in the month

August.reason: Driest, most stable east-side conditions with dry talus

September.reason: Short clear window remains but weather becomes less reliable as fall approaches

weather.typical: Drier east-side (Chelan/Holden) climate than the west-side Cascades; cold and exposed at elevation even in summer
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms can develop over the Glacier Peak Wilderness high country in summer; approach and summit day should account for a bail-out plan on ridge/talus terrain

backups.rope_note: Carry a rope and a few slings. This route's own gear list holds both, for the optional rappel near the summit: there is a fixed anchor up there that lets a party past the crux Class 4 step without downclimbing it. The rest of the west ridge is Class 3 scrambling on loose schist and is not roped, and the rock is crumbly the whole way, so a helmet matters more than a rack here.
rack: Light rack: a few small-to-mid cams and nuts
A few slings for natural anchors (horns, chockstones, trees)
30-60m rope for the crux gully / exposed step near the summit

approach_variants.name: Holden Village to Holden Pass, then east up the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Access is by Lake Chelan ferry from Chelan or Field's Point Landing to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up eleven miles of gravel road and twelve switchbacks into the village. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood; confirm they are running before anything else.

From the village, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 runs a mile up-valley to the fork, then the Holden Lake Trail climbs about four miles and 1,700 ft to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft. Above the lake the climbers' path gains a further 1,100 ft over heather benches and rocky terraces to Holden Pass near 6,400 ft. This is the same camp Bonanza's routes use, and it is effectively the last water.

The rock on this route is loose crumbly schist and marble all the way up, and parties route-find by cairn rather than by feature. There is a fixed rappel anchor near the top for the crux step.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable
hazards: Loose, crumbly schist and marble across the entire route, on and off the crest
A short, exposed Class 4 step just below the summit — a fixed anchor is present but is not maintained by anyone
One gully looking exactly like the next on a route where cairns, not features, are the navigation
Sharing a camp with Bonanza parties and a pass with two mountains' worth of routes leaving it in opposite directions
Ferry and shuttle access to Holden Village, closed since the December 2025 flood
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Holden Pass serves two mountains and the direction you leave it is the whole route-finding problem. The pass is the saddle between Bonanza and Martin. Bonanza's routes go west from it, onto benches and the Mary Green Glacier. Martin's West Ridge goes east, straight up out of the pass. If you are traversing toward a glacier, you are on Bonanza's ground.

So the base is the pass itself: no approach across a glacier, no basin, no traverse. The ridge rises directly out of the saddle and the scrambling starts where the heather runs out.

The positive test is which side of the crest you are on, and it repeats. Gain the ridge by a series of gullies and scramble on the right — the south — side of the crest, then repeat that pattern upward. Right side, gully, back toward the crest, right side again. A party on the north flank has left the route, and the north side of this crest is not the easier ground.

In fog, follow cairns here rather than features. The rock is uniformly crumbly schist and beige marble and one gully looks like the next; on this particular route cairn-following is the documented method rather than a bad habit. That is the opposite of the advice for the scramble on Mount Pugh, where cairns lead to cliffs — do not carry one peak's rule to the other.

The arrival at the crux is an anchor, which is rare on this mountain. About 100 ft below the summit a steep, exposed Class 4 gully is the route's hardest ground, with good holds, and a fixed rappel anchor has been observed beside it. Finding fixed hardware on this peak means you are 100 ft from the top and on the standard line. Finding none, on ground much harder than Class 4, means you are not.

The loose beige-marble gully partway up is the other named feature and it is on the south side of the crest, so it doubles as a position check: you should meet it while traversing right, not while on the crest.

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is closed to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party
